abstract: OpenAI Economic Research's second entry in its Work at the Frontier series (Caroline Chin, Alex Martin Richmond, July 27 2026) asks not whether AI can do a task, but who ends up doing it. Using a random sample of over 800,000 work-related messages from individual ChatGPT accounts of US users whose occupations were linked via ChatGPT Business role data, the authors classify each message to a single O*NET detailed work activity and compare it with the sender's stated occupation. They label the result task crossover: work historically associated with one occupation appearing in the AI use of people in another. Across eight occupation groups (customer experience, design, engineering, finance, HR, legal, marketing, sales), 16.8% of all work-related messages and 43.5% of occupation-specific messages concern tasks historically associated with another occupation; 21.8% are within-occupation and 61.5% are generic work shared broadly across jobs. Cross-occupation work is the majority of occupation-specific messages in five of eight groups. The paper's most useful structural finding is that borrowing and lending are distinct: designers draw heavily on other fields (35.2% of their messages) while design work almost never appears elsewhere (1.7%), whereas engineering is the inverse. Marketing leads in both directions. The report extends OpenAI's AI Jobs Transition Framework, which argued that a significant share of jobs will reorganize rather than disappear, and it is explicit that this is descriptive evidence about the division of labor — not an employment or productivity estimate.
keyFindings: 16.8% of all work-related messages, and 43.5% of occupation-specific (non-generic) messages, concern tasks historically associated with another occupation; 21.8% within-occupation, 61.5% generic
Cross-occupation work is the majority of occupation-specific messages in five of eight groups: customer experience 77%, design 75%, HR 69%, legal 56%, marketing 53%

Borrowing and lending are independent: designers draw 35.2% of their messages from other occupations but design tasks are only 1.7% of others' messages; engineering is the inverse (18.5% borrowed in, 7.4% traveling out)
Marketing leads both directions — 24.3% of marketers' messages are cross-occupation, and marketing tasks are 8.9% of other occupations' messages, the highest outbound share in the sample
Two tasks travel universally: calculating financial data and troubleshooting computer applications each rank top-three in all seven non-native occupation groups
Smaller workspaces show more crossover among typical-volume users: 18.9% at 2-5 seats vs 16.3% at 101+ seats (~2.5pp, roughly 13% relative); the gradient is not monotonic among top-quartile users

The authors flag a measurement implication: if AI changes which workers perform which tasks, statistics built on existing job descriptions will progressively diverge from how work is actually organized
methodology: Random sample of 800,000+ work-related messages from individual ChatGPT accounts of US users, with occupation assigned from self-reported Department/Role data in the users' linked ChatGPT Business accounts; users without that data are dropped, as are users whose role maps to more than one of the eight groups. Classification is hierarchical: each eligible message is assigned one O*NET Intermediate Work Activity, then a Detailed Work Activity drawn from that IWA or one of the five most semantically similar IWAs by title embedding. Occupational boundaries are built from an employment-weighted occupation-to-SOC crosswalk plus O*NET task links, task ratings, and DWA embeddings; a DWA falls inside a boundary if directly linked or if cosine similarity to the nearest boundary DWA is at least 0.80. Messages are then labeled Generic, Within occupation, or Cross-occupation. Up to nine preceding messages provide classification context, but only the selected message is labeled. Messages are classified by model; the authors state they never read underlying messages.
qualifiers: Tier 2 — first-party company research using proprietary product logs, not peer-reviewed and not independently replicable. The limitations are unusually well-stated by the authors and should be carried into any citation. The unit of analysis is a message, explicitly 'not an hour of work, a completed project, or a job,' so message shares cannot be read as shares of time, output, or employment. The sample is not representative of the US workforce: it is ChatGPT Business-linked users in eight white-collar occupation groups, and the authors note ChatGPT Business and Enterprise are separate product populations whose results should not be generalized to one another. Occupation is self-reported. The study observes requests, not outcomes — it does not capture whether output was used, whether it was any good, how much time it saved, whether the user could have done the task unaided, or whether a specialist reviewed it. Results are descriptive and do not reveal how the same workers would have allocated tasks without AI. The report states directly: 'This study maps AI-aided work; it does not estimate AI's effect on employment or productivity,' and that findings should be read 'as evidence that the division of work is shifting, not as direct estimates of which occupations will gain or lose jobs.' Workspace seat count is a proxy for many things (specialization, industry, organizational maturity) and is not company size. Because a message may contain multiple overlapping tasks, the assigned DWA is its primary activity only.
